findings.title: CloudSEK reports reconstructed exposure from LiteLLM supply-chain compromise
findings.concise_factual_summary: CloudSEK published a reconstructed exposure dataset for the March 2026 LiteLLM compromise, reporting 2,500+ companies and about 434,000 CI/CD pipelines potentially exposed. The report says compromised runners could expose SSH keys, cloud credentials, Kubernetes tokens, .env files, CI/CD secrets, LLM API keys, and AI gateway configuration; it cautions that exposure counts are not proof every organization was compromised.
findings.evidence_classification: primary security research with corroborating reputable security coverage
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: LiteLLM PyPI releases 1.82.7 and 1.82.8; CI/CD runners and AI infrastructure secrets reachable during the March 2026 exposure window
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: LiteLLM is an AI gateway/proxy component. A malicious package at that control point can bridge dependency supply chain, identity, cloud runtime, CI/CD, and model-provider credential exposure, making AI infrastructure a high-value lateral-movement target.

upstream_routing.route_note: Broad LiteLLM, Trivy, PyPI, CloudSEK, and provider/company catalog facts belong upstream if durable entity pages are needed.

General CI/CD, package pinning, and development workflow lessons belong upstream as AI-assisted development practice; this repo should keep AI security supply-chain implications, exposed AI secrets, and incident-response controls.

findings.confidence_notes: High confidence on visible dates and primary CloudSEK claims. CloudSEK and secondary coverage warn that the exposure dataset is not equivalent to confirmed compromise of every named organization.
follow_up_actions: During ingest, distinguish reconstructed exposure from confirmed compromise.
Check whether existing local pages cover AI gateway supply-chain credential rotation and long-lived token retirement.
Track any later LiteLLM, Aqua, FBI, or PyPI primary updates that refine root cause or victim impact.

findings.title: Researchers disclose cross-model replay attack against encrypted reasoning traces

visible_dates.date: Published yesterday in search result for the 2026-08-12 run
No explicit publication date fetched; paper states provider behavior was assessed as of July 2026 and reports responsible disclosure before in-window coverage
visible_dates.date_type: undated primary paper with in-window secondary coverage

findings.concise_factual_summary: The paper 'Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs' describes an architectural weakness where encrypted reasoning blocks were portable across sessions, users, and models within a provider ecosystem. Researchers report using weaker compatible models as decoders for reasoning traces from stronger models across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google; from 315,320 public reasoning blocks they recovered 367 PII artifacts and 182 credentials. WIRED reports providers were alerted and mitigations have been applied, while some trace recovery may remain possible.
findings.evidence_classification: public research paper qualified by in-window reputable security/news coverage
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: Client-side encrypted reasoning blocks and thinking signatures in proprietary reasoning APIs; provider/model compatibility conditions vary by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google model family
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: Encrypted hidden reasoning can contain credentials, PII, tool outputs, policy-sensitive refusal reasoning, and invisible prompt-injection payloads. Client-side storage and cross-context replay make reasoning traces a data-security, model-IP, and agent-rollout integrity boundary, not just a UX implementation detail.
named_entities: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems

upstream_routing.route_note: Broad model-family and provider facts for Claude, GPT, Gemini, Kimi, and GLM belong upstream.

General logging, session transcript hygiene, and developer workflow guidance for not publishing opaque reasoning blocks belongs upstream; this repo should keep security implications for reasoning confidentiality, credential leakage, and prompt-injection channels.

findings.confidence_notes: Medium-high confidence. The primary paper was fetched but did not expose a clear publication date; in-window qualification relies on WIRED and The Hacker News coverage dated within the collection window.
follow_up_actions: During ingest, avoid reproducing exploit prompts or recovered secret examples.
Track provider postmortems or official mitigation advisories if OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google publish them.
Consider a local security lens for encrypted reasoning blocks as sensitive artifacts in agent logs.

findings.concise_factual_summary: CSA's 2026 Top Threats to Cloud Computing Survey Report says identity, AI, third-party resources, and API threats dominate the cloud threat landscape. It states two AI security risks enter the rankings for the first time: AI-Enhanced Attacks, covering adversarial use of AI to improve and automate attacks, and AI System Compromise, covering manipulation or abuse of AI models, data, agents, tools, and pipelines.
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: Cloud security risk management, identity and access management, AI systems, agents, tools, pipelines, APIs, third-party dependencies, and CSA AI Cloud Controls Matrix v1.1 mappings
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: The report makes AI system compromise and AI-enabled attacker automation first-class cloud threats, tying AI security to identity, APIs, third-party dependencies, software development, cloud data, visibility, change control, and resilience.

findings.title: NIST seeks feedback on AI-enabled vulnerability management and NVD modernization
findings.concise_factual_summary: NIST published a Cybersecurity Insights post seeking feedback on AI-enabled vulnerability management and NVD modernization. The post says AI creates opportunities to discover and exploit vulnerabilities and to strengthen cybersecurity response, and that NIST wants to improve NVD scalability, automation, interoperability, transparency, and utility. It also says NIST has begun V-etalon, an AI-assisted tool for enriching vulnerability information, and asks for feedback in areas including vulnerability data and standards, remediation deployment and monitoring, and development processes by October 13, 2026.
findings.evidence_classification: official government cybersecurity standards and vulnerability-management source
findings.affected_boundary_or_version: NVD, vulnerability information enrichment, vulnerability management process, remediation monitoring, CPE specifications, and AI-enabled cyber tooling
findings.why_it_matters_for_ai_security: AI security assurance depends on trustworthy vulnerability metadata for model-serving stacks, agent tools, dependencies, AI infrastructure, and AI-enabled vulnerability discovery. NIST is explicitly tying AI-enabled cyber capabilities to continuous, contextual, automated vulnerability management.

General vulnerability-management workflow modernization and development-process implications route upstream; this repo should keep AI security standards, assurance, and vulnerability-data implications.
